 No fixed salary, no fixed pension: Is India's retirement system ready for gig workers?
 With gig work, freelancing and job switches becoming increasingly common, India's pension ecosystem needs to move beyond fixed monthly contributions. Retirees, meanwhile, need more flexible withdrawal options that can protect their income against inflation and rising longevity 
 Navneet Dubey 
 November 19, 2026 / 10:17 IST

 India's gig workforce increased from 77 lakh in 2020-21 to 1.2 crore in 2024-25, registering a 55 percent increase over four years, according to the Economic Survey 2025-26. 
 Gig work growth demands flexible pension systems in India.
 Traditional fixed monthly schemes fail irregular earners.
 Retirement products need inflation and longevity protection.

 With gig work, freelancing and job switches becoming increasingly common, India's pension ecosystem needs to move beyond fixed monthly contributions. Retirees, meanwhile, need more flexible annuity options that can protect their income against inflation and rising longevity.
 The retirement planning system was largely built around a predictable career path: Get a salaried job, contribute regularly to a provident fund, accumulate savings over the years and use the corpus to fund life after retirement. But what happens when there is no fixed salary, no employer making retirement contributions and no certainty about next month's income?
 Story continues below Advertisement 
 Remove Ad 
 This is becoming an increasingly relevant question as more Indians take up gig work, freelancing, consulting and self-employment, or move frequently between employers. For these workers, the traditional approach to retirement savings may not always work.
 The scale of this shift is significant. India's gig workforce increased from 77 lakh in 2020-21 to 1.2 crore in 2024-25, registering a 55 percent increase over four years, according to the Economic Survey 2025-26. The workforce is projected to grow further, with non-agricultural gig workers expected to account for 6.7 percent of the total workforce by 2029-30.
 The expansion raises an important question: Is India's retirement architecture adapting quickly enough to accommodate people whose earnings are irregular, employment arrangements are fluid and retirement savings cannot depend on a fixed monthly contribution?
 Story continues below Advertisement 
 Remove Ad 
 “India's workforce is becoming increasingly diverse, but retirement planning has historically been structured around predictable monthly salaries, stable employment and employer-linked contributions. That model does not adequately reflect the realities of a growing section of the workforce," said Vishwajeet Goel, Head of Pensionbazaar.

 Retirement planning cannot depend on a fixed salary 
 Traditional retirement products have largely been designed around predictable earnings, stable employment and employer-linked contributions. Employees in the organised sector can build retirement savings through mechanisms such as the Employees' Provident Fund (EPF), while those outside this structure must take greater responsibility for their long-term financial security.

 Remove Ad 
 For a self-employed professional, freelancer or gig worker, income may fluctuate considerably from one month to another. There may be months of higher earnings followed by periods of limited work. Someone moving between salaried employment and independent work may also find it difficult to maintain a consistent retirement-saving routine.
 "The problem is not necessarily a lack of willingness to save. Rather, conventional retirement products may not adequately accommodate irregular cash flows," said Goel.
 "This makes flexibility an important consideration in the design of pension products. Workers should ideally be able to increase contributions when earnings are higher, make smaller contributions during lean periods and resume saving without facing unnecessary restrictions," he added.
 Portable retirement accounts are equally important. As individuals move between employers, platforms and independent work arrangements, their retirement savings should continue accumulating without requiring them to start afresh every time their employment status changes.
 The National Pension System (NPS) is one avenue through which individuals can build a market-linked retirement corpus outside traditional employer-linked arrangements. Its voluntary structure and digital access can make it relevant to self-employed individuals as well. However, awareness, affordability and the ability to contribute consistently remain important considerations.
 There are also policy-level efforts to widen pension coverage. The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) introduced the NPS e-Shramik model in October 2025 to bring gig and platform workers into the pension system. The regulator subsequently extended the incentive framework for the model to FY27.
 The government's broader social security framework has also recognised gig and platform workers. The Code on Social Security, 2020, which came into force on November 21, 2025, provides for social security measures covering life and disability protection, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits and old-age protection. However, the actual benefits available to workers will depend on the schemes framed and implemented under the Code; its provisions should not be interpreted as an automatic guarantee of a pension for every gig worker.
 The challenge, therefore, is to translate policy recognition into accessible and meaningful retirement savings options.

 Small, flexible contributions could make a difference 
 One of the biggest hurdles in retirement planning for workers with irregular earnings is the pressure to commit to a fixed contribution every month.
 A gig worker may earn substantially more during one month and considerably less in another. A freelancer may receive payments only after completing projects, while a self-employed professional may have to prioritise business expenses and working capital before setting aside money for retirement.
 Pension products need to account for these realities. Flexible contribution schedules, low minimum investment requirements, simple digital enrolment and the ability to pause and restart contributions could encourage more people to participate.
 Financial awareness is another challenge. Many individuals prioritise immediate financial goals, such as buying a house, repaying loans or building an emergency fund, but postpone retirement planning because it appears distant. For workers without employer-backed retirement benefits, this delay could have a greater impact.
 Starting early, even with relatively small contributions, can help individuals benefit from a longer investment horizon. However, the contribution strategy must also account for income volatility, emergency savings and other financial obligations.
 Retiring is one challenge; generating income is another 
 Retirement planning does not end with building a corpus. Individuals must ensure their savings generate income for decades. Annuities help by converting a lump sum into regular income, but traditional products offer limited choices.
 “Retirees are not a homogeneous group. Someone retiring at 58 with other investments and family responsibilities has very different requirements from someone retiring at 70 who prioritises predictable monthly income. The industry needs to move towards greater personalisation in annuity design,” said Goel.
 Products need flexible payouts, inflation protection, spouse benefits, liquidity and greater transparency. Financial awareness is equally important, as retirement security cannot depend solely on formal salaried employment.
 Also read EPFO may widen post-retirement corpus withdrawal choices 
 Can withdrawal plans become more flexible? 
 There is growing recognition within the pension industry that retirement-income products need to evolve.
 One possible direction is to combine guaranteed annuity income with systematic withdrawal solutions. This could allow retirees to secure a basic income stream while keeping another portion of their retirement corpus invested and accessible for future expenses.
 The National Pension System's Retirement Income Scheme (RIS), introduced in 2026, is another development in this direction. It allows eligible retirees to receive systematic payouts from their withdrawable NPS corpus while the remaining funds continue to be invested. However, these payouts remain market-linked and are not equivalent to a guaranteed annuity.
 “Such solutions could offer retirees greater control over how they use their accumulated savings, but they also require clear communication about market risks, withdrawal rates and the possibility of exhausting the corpus,” said Goel.
